items.label: What returned: after a break, in a new context

brief.situation: You are a licensed psychologist. Elena Ruiz, 34 (a fictional client), was rear-ended at a highway on-ramp seven months ago, without serious injury, and developed a fear of driving; at intake you diagnosed a specific phobia and screened out PTSD. Over five sessions of graded exposure she drove her neighborhood and a city arterial with little fear. Then she took a two-week vacation. Today is session six. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Exposure so far: parked car, neighborhood loops, a city arterial at midday, each repeated until her fear dropped; her husband rode along for the first three.
She starts a new job across town next month; the fastest route uses the highway.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Elena answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'How did the two weeks go?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Vacation was great. Then I came back and tried to drive to the new office." She shakes her head. "It's all come back. Therapy didn't work."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Elena nods hard. "I was so proud of the arterial. Now I feel like a fraud."

askWhat.label: Ask her to walk you through the drive: where, when, and what happened

effects.log: You ask her to describe the drive step by step.

effects.finding: "Saturday, my first drive since before vacation. A route I'd never done, toward the highway. At the on-ramp my heart went crazy and I pulled over. My neighborhood's still fine. I drove to the store yesterday, no problem."

askNewEvent.label: Ask whether anything frightening actually happened on the drive or since: a near miss, another crash, bad news
askNewEvent.available: not talking and (contextKnown and not newEventAsked)

effects.log: You ask whether anything new and frightening happened.

effects.finding: "No. Nobody came close. I just panicked."

effects.log: No new aversive event, so this is not reinstatement: the fear returned with time and a new context.

askWider.label: Ask where else the fear shows up now: riding as a passenger, sounds, anything that reminds her of the crash
askWider.available: not talking and (contextKnown and not genKnown)

effects.log: You ask where else the fear appears.

effects.finding: "I tense up riding with my husband now, especially merging. And screeching brakes on TV make me jump. That never used to bother me."

explainReturn.label: Explain that exposure builds new learning, not an erasure: fear often returns after a break and in a new place, and that is expected, not failure
explainReturn.available: not talking and (contextKnown and not explainedReturn)

effects.log: You explain how extinction works: a new 'safe' memory competes with the old fear one; time away and a new context favor the old one.

effects.finding: She sits back. "So I didn't lose it. The new learning just didn't come with me to a new road."

effects.log: Return of fear after time (spontaneous recovery) and in a new context (renewal) is expected when extinction is new learning (Craske et al. 2014).

askPrediction.label: Ask what she predicts would happen if she drove onto the on-ramp and merged
askPrediction.available: not talking and (contextKnown and not expectancyElicited)

effects.log: You ask her to name exactly what she expects would happen.

effects.finding: "I'd panic, freeze, and someone would hit me. Like before."

askSafety.label: Ask what she does to feel safer while driving
askSafety.available: not talking and (contextKnown and not safetyKnown)

effects.log: You ask about the things she does to get through a drive.

effects.finding: "Right lane only. Radio off. Text my husband when I leave and when I arrive. And I grip the wheel at ten and two the whole time."

planExposure.label: Plan this week's exposure with her: the on-ramp and new routes, different times of day, short spaced drives, her prediction tested, safety behaviors dropped one by one
planExposure.available: not talking and (explainedReturn and not planVaried)
planExposure.why: Planned (explain the return of fear first).

effects.log: You build a varied plan with her consent: on-ramps and unfamiliar routes, mornings and evenings, short drives several times a week, each one testing her prediction, the safety behaviors dropped step by step.

effects.finding: "Tuesday morning, the on-ramp by the mall, merge and exit at the next one. Radio on. No text." She writes it down.

effects.log: Variability, multiple contexts, expectancy violation and dropping safety behaviors are what make extinction learning travel (Craske et al. 2014).

flood.label: Tell her the fastest fix is to drive the highway at rush hour this week and stay on it until the fear is gone

effects.log: You propose a long highway drive at rush hour.

effects.finding: "Are you serious? I couldn't get on the ramp."

effects.log: An intensity she has not agreed to, at the top of her hierarchy, risks escape and more fear; exposure is planned with her consent (APA 3.10).

relaxInstead.label: Suggest stopping exposure for now and switching to relaxation training

effects.log: You suggest setting exposure aside for relaxation work.
Return of fear is not a reason to drop exposure; avoiding the cue leaves the old learning in charge.

reassure.label: Reassure her that nothing bad will happen on the highway

effects.log: You promise her she will be fine on the highway.
Reassurance does not test her prediction; it becomes one more safety signal.

takeBus.label: Agree she should take the bus to the new job for now, until she feels ready

effects.log: You agree she can avoid driving there for now.

effects.finding: She looks relieved. "Okay. Maybe in the spring."

agreeFailed.label: Agree that exposure may not have worked for her
agreeFailed.available: not talking and (storyHeard and not agreedFailed)

effects.log: You agree that exposure may not suit her.

blame.label: Ask whether she skipped her practice drives during vacation

effects.log: You ask if she practiced while away.

effects.finding: "It was a vacation. We flew." Her jaw tightens.

effects.log: You close the session and set the next appointment.

document.label: Document the formulation and the plan

options.label: Return of fear after a two-week break and on a new route (spontaneous recovery, renewal); generalized to riding as a passenger and to brake sounds; her neighborhood still safe (discrimination)
Exposure did not work; the fear was never extinguished
Resume exposure this week: on-ramps and new routes, varied times, spaced drives, predictions tested, safety behaviors dropped
Highway at rush hour this week until the fear is gone
Bus for now; revisit driving later

why.title: Predict (not scored)
why.context: Her fear came back on her first drive after a two-week break, on a route she had never practiced, with nothing new happening. Her neighborhood is still fine. What best explains it?

choices.label: Spontaneous recovery and renewal: extinction learning is tied to time and context

effects.log: Prediction: spontaneous recovery and renewal.

choices.feedback: Right. Extinction is new learning that competes with the old fear; it weakens with time since practice (spontaneous recovery) and outside the practiced context (renewal). Her neighborhood still working is discrimination (Craske et al. 2014).

choices.label: The exposure failed; the fear was never extinguished

effects.log: Prediction: exposure failed.

choices.feedback: Unlikely. Her neighborhood and the arterial are still fine, so extinction happened; it just did not carry to a new road after a break.

choices.label: Reinstatement: something new and frightening happened

effects.log: Prediction: reinstatement.

choices.feedback: Only if an aversive event occurred, and nothing did. Ask, then name what fits: time and a new context.

formulation.question: Write your formulation in conditioning terms, and the plan that follows from it.

parts.label: The conditioning account
parts.criteria: Acquisition: the on-ramp crash (US) conditioned fear to driving cues (CS); generalization to riding and brake sounds; extinction through exposure is new inhibitory learning; its return after a two-week break (spontaneous recovery) and on a new route (renewal), with no new aversive event (not reinstatement); the neighborhood still safe (discrimination).
parts.modelAnswer: The crash at an on-ramp paired driving cues with an aversive event, and fear was acquired to them; it has generalized to riding as a passenger and to brake sounds, while her neighborhood stays safe (discrimination). Exposure built new inhibitory learning rather than erasing the old association, so after a two-week break (spontaneous recovery) and on an unpracticed route (renewal) the old learning won out. Nothing frightening happened, so this is not reinstatement.

parts.label: The plan
parts.criteria: Normalize return of fear; resume exposure promptly with her consent; vary routes, times and contexts including on-ramps; spaced practice; test her stated prediction (expectancy violation); drop safety behaviors; no flooding without consent, no switching away from exposure, no reassurance or endorsed avoidance.
parts.modelAnswer: I told her this is expected, not failure. With her agreement we resume this week with short, spaced drives on new routes and at different times, starting at an on-ramp, each one a test of her prediction that she will freeze and be hit, and we drop the right-lane rule, the silent radio and the check-in texts one at a time. Reassurance, a switch to relaxation alone, or taking the bus would keep the old learning in charge.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Not used by this case's endings: the case is judged on the formulation and the plan.

walkout.narrative: Elena left mid-session, sure now that she is back at the start.

flooded.when: documented and not walkedOut and (floodNow or planDoc == "flood")
flooded.narrative: The plan asks Elena to do the hardest drive on her list this week, which she did not agree to. If she escapes it, the fear learns one more time that the highway is dangerous.

abandoned.when: documented and not walkedOut and planDoc != "variedExposure"
abandoned.narrative: Driving is set aside for now. Every week of avoidance gives the old fear learning more room; the new job's commute starts next month.

expertPath.text: Check in and reflect; walk through the drive: after a break, a new route; ask whether anything new happened, and where else the fear shows up.
Explain return of fear: extinction is new learning, tied to time and context; this is expected.
Name her prediction and her safety behaviors; plan varied, spaced exposure starting at an on-ramp, with her consent.
Document the conditioning formulation and the plan.

backOnTrack.headline: Good: return of fear understood and used
backOnTrack.body: You found that the fear returned after time and in a new context with nothing new happening, explained it as expected, and built a varied plan that tests her prediction and drops safety behaviors.

gaps.headline: Exposure resumes, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was missing in the assessment, the explanation or the plan.

walkout.headline: She left
walkout.body: A client who feels she has failed needs the return of fear explained, not blame or a harder assignment.

flooded.headline: Flooding without consent
flooded.body: Exposure intensity is agreed with the client. Pushing to the top of her hierarchy now risks escape, which teaches the fear again.

abandoned.headline: Exposure abandoned
abandoned.body: Return of fear after a break or in a new place is expected when extinction is new learning; stepping away from exposure, or into avoidance, lets the old learning win (Craske et al. 2014).

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: The crash conditioned fear to driving cues, and it has generalized to riding as a passenger and to brake sounds, while her neighborhood stays safe (discrimination). Exposure produced extinction, which is new inhibitory learning, not erasure. After two weeks without practice (spontaneous recovery) and on an unpracticed route (renewal) the old fear returned; nothing aversive happened, so it is not reinstatement. Explain that this is expected. Resume exposure with her consent, varied in routes, times and contexts (starting at an on-ramp), spaced, each drive testing her stated prediction, with safety behaviors dropped. Avoid flooding without consent, reassurance, switching to relaxation alone, or endorsing avoidance.
